paper_metadata.title: Benchmarking Amplitude Estimation on a Superconducting Quantum Computer

summary: The paper benchmarks Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE) on the 7‑qubit IBM Nairobi superconducting device using inner‑product circuits for 2‑ and 4‑dimensional unit vectors. Optimized compilation (Qiskit level‑3 and Pytket level‑2) enabled circuits with depth ~131 for 3 Grover iterations and achieved a best mean error of 0.0442 for the 4‑qubit case, while the 2‑qubit case reached ~0.0017 error. Results show MLAE outperforming naive sampling on these small benchmarks but remain far from the ~54 million T‑depth estimated for real quantum advantage in Monte Carlo finance tasks.

experiments.description: Benchmarking maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation (MLAE) for estimating the inner product amplitude of two 2-dimensional unit vectors on IBM Nairobi, comparing ordinary transpilation, optimized transpilation, and naive sampling.

algorithm.variant: Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE) with linear incremental sequence (LIS) schedule
algorithm.parameter_initialization: uniform distribution over theta in [0, pi/2]

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Unary data-loader / inner-product circuit; amplitude of the first qubit encodes the squared inner product of two 2D unit vectors
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the amplitude a of a prepared quantum state, where sin^2(theta)=a and a corresponds to the squared inner product of two unit vectors

problem_instance.description: Inner product estimation for two 2-dimensional unit vectors

dataset_specification.description: Example vectors given in paper; one instance shown with a=[-0.96184207, 0.27360523], b=[0.96845237, 0.24919873]

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Random unit vectors generated; inner product uniformly distributed
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 500 shots per Grover-iteration circuit, repeated 50 times; compared MLE output and naive sampling against exact inner product; mean relative error reported

transpilation_settings.optimization_level: standard transpilation vs aggressive optimization (Qiskit level 3 and Pytket level 2)

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Random unit-vector generation; construction of inner-product circuits; compilation with Qiskit and Pytket
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation over theta; naive sampling baseline; relative error computation

speedup_claims.conditions: 2-qubit inner-product estimation on IBM Nairobi; up to 7 Grover iterations; 500 shots per iteration; averaged over 50 repetitions
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide a numeric naive-sampling error for the 2-qubit case in text; it only states that both ordinary and optimized circuits outperformed naive sampling.

speedup_claims.conditions: Amplitude estimation convergence versus classical sampling
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a general AE property stated in the introduction, not a measured speedup from the experiment.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: unknown; paper provides no scaling analysis beyond toy circuits
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Authors cite prior work estimating ~54 million T-depth required for practical quantum advantage in Monte Carlo finance applications.
limiting_factors: hardware noise limits useful Grover iterations

notes: Paper explicitly states IBM Nairobi superconducting computer with 7 qubits, but this experiment uses a 2-qubit inner-product circuit; num_qubits set to the circuit register size for the experiment.
Circuit depth for the 2-qubit case is not explicitly given; only qualitative depth comparisons and a 4-qubit depth example are reported elsewhere.
Authors compare MLAE with naive sampling and show lower error for a toy 2‑qubit experiment, but do not claim practical quantum advantage.
Problem size is trivial and does not outperform classical Monte Carlo in realistic settings.

experiments.description: Benchmarking MLAE for estimating the inner product amplitude of two 4-dimensional unit vectors on IBM Nairobi, comparing ordinary transpilation, optimized transpilation (Qiskit and Pytket), and naive sampling.

algorithm.variant: Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE) with linear incremental sequence (LIS) schedule
algorithm.parameter_initialization: uniform distribution over theta in [0, pi/2]

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Unary data-loader / inner-product circuit; 4 basis states encode a 4-dimensional unit vector, and the amplitude of |0001> encodes the squared inner product
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the amplitude a of a prepared quantum state, where a corresponds to the squared inner product of two 4-dimensional unit vectors

problem_instance.description: Inner product estimation for two random 4-dimensional unit vectors

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Random unit vectors generated; inner product uniformly distributed
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 50 random vector pairs; 500 shots per Grover-iteration circuit; repeated 50 times; compared MLE and naive sampling against exact inner product; mean error reported

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Random unit-vector generation; construction of 4D inner-product circuits; compilation with Qiskit and Pytket
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation over theta; naive sampling baseline; relative error computation

speedup_claims.conditions: 4-dimensional unit-vector inner-product estimation on IBM Nairobi; 500 shots per Grover-iteration circuit; up to 7 Grover iterations; averaged over 50 repetitions
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide a numeric naive-sampling error in text for the 4D case, only that MLE outperformed naive sampling.

speedup_claims.conditions: Amplitude estimation convergence versus classical sampling

limiting_factors: hardware noise and decoherence limit Grover iterations beyond ~3
circuit depths already ~131–300 at only 4 qubits
quadratic speedup insufficient given fault‑tolerant overhead

notes: The paper explicitly reports a best result for the 4-qubit experiment at depth 131 for 3 Grover iterations; this is used as the circuit depth for the optimized 4D experiment.
The paper does not provide a full gate count breakdown for the 4D experiment, so those fields are null.
MLAE shows lower error than naive sampling on 4‑qubit circuits, but this is a small-scale benchmark rather than a practical computational advantage.
Authors explicitly state that current hardware is far from the threshold for quantum advantage.
